metaTitle: Event-Based Automation: Event-Driven vs Scheduled Workflows
metaDescription: Event-driven automation starts a workflow the moment something happens, like a new email. See how it differs from scheduled runs and which events trigger GAIA.
definition: Event-driven automation (also called event-based automation) runs a workflow the moment something happens, such as a new email arriving, an issue being created or a row being added to a spreadsheet, instead of at a fixed time. Each automation pairs a trigger event with the actions to take, and the system where the event happened notifies the automation platform, usually through a webhook.
extendedDescription:
Traditional automation runs on schedules: every hour, every morning, every Monday. Event-driven automation runs on events: the moment a new email arrives, a task is created, a Slack message is posted, or a calendar event changes. This shift from polling to event-driven processing enables near-instant response times and eliminates the latency of waiting for the next scheduled run.

Event-driven automation is built on webhooks and message queues. When an event occurs in an external system, that system sends a notification to the automation platform (via webhook or message queue), which then routes the event to the appropriate workflow. This push-based architecture is more efficient than polling APIs repeatedly to check for changes.

For AI agents, event-driven architecture enables proactive behavior. The agent does not wait for you to ask a question; it acts the moment a relevant event occurs. When an urgent email arrives at 11 PM, an event-driven AI can triage it and alert you immediately rather than discovering it during the next morning's scheduled check.

Event-driven systems require careful consideration of event ordering, idempotency (handling the same event twice safely), and error recovery (what happens if the workflow fails partway through). Message queues like RabbitMQ provide the durability and ordering guarantees needed for reliable event-driven automation.

Anatomy of an event-driven workflow: a trigger (the event type, such as a new GitHub issue), filters or conditions (only issues labelled bug, only emails from a client's domain), actions (summarize, create a task, post to Slack, draft a reply) and error handling (retry, alert or skip). Good automations also deduplicate, because many providers deliver the same webhook more than once.

Push vs polling: a true push trigger arrives through a webhook seconds after the event. Many integrations poll instead: the platform asks the source for changes at an interval, so a polling trigger is near real time rather than instant. When a tool offers no trigger at all, the fallback is a scheduled run that checks for changes.

Event-driven vs scheduled: choose events when the value is in reacting fast (triaging an urgent email, routing a new lead, acknowledging a support request). Choose a schedule for a batch at a known time (a morning digest, a weekly report) or when the source has no trigger. Most real setups use both, and the hard case is overlap: when a record can match a real-time trigger and a scheduled batch, give it an idempotency key or a processed flag so it is handled once.

Event-driven automation tools: Zapier, Make, n8n and Pipedream are the common general-purpose platforms, each letting you pick a trigger app and chain actions. Cloud services such as AWS EventBridge route events between systems for engineering teams. AI assistants add a different layer: the workflow is described in plain language, and an agent decides how to carry it out each time the event fires.
howGaiaUsesIt: GAIA workflows can start from an integration event. Supported triggers include new and sent Gmail messages, Google Calendar events being created or about to start, Slack messages, GitHub commits, pull requests, issues and stars, Linear issues and comments, new Asana and Todoist tasks, new or updated Notion pages, new rows in Google Sheets, and new, updated or deleted Google Docs. Events reach GAIA through Composio's webhook; GAIA matches each one to the workflows subscribed to it and queues a background run on ARQ, its Redis-based job queue. Some triggers, Gmail among them, are polled at an interval rather than pushed, so near real time is the accurate description. Tools without a trigger, such as Trello, HubSpot or Jira, can still be handled on a schedule you set.

faqs.question: How is event-driven automation different from scheduled automation?
faqs.answer: Scheduled automation runs at fixed times whether or not anything happened. Event-driven automation runs when a specific event occurs, so the reaction follows the event instead of waiting for the next run. GAIA supports both: a workflow can start from an integration event, such as a new Gmail message or a new GitHub issue, or on a schedule.

faqs.question: What events can trigger GAIA workflows?
faqs.answer: Integration events from Gmail (new and sent messages), Google Calendar (event created, event starting soon), Slack (new messages, with options to skip bot messages, DMs or thread replies), GitHub (commits, pull requests, issues, stars), Linear (issues created or updated, comments), Asana and Todoist (new tasks), Notion (new or updated pages), Google Sheets (new rows or sheets) and Google Docs (new, updated or deleted documents). Other tools, such as Trello, HubSpot or Jira, can be checked on a schedule instead.

faqs.question: What are examples of event-driven automation?
faqs.answer: A new support email creates a task and a draft reply. A new GitHub issue labelled bug posts a summary to the team's Slack channel. A calendar event that is about to start triggers a briefing on the attendees. A new row in a leads spreadsheet gets researched and assigned to a salesperson.

faqs.question: How do I run an AI workflow from an external trigger?
faqs.answer: Connect the app that produces the event, create a workflow, pick that app's trigger (for example a new Linear issue), add any filters and describe in plain language what should happen. In GAIA, each time the event fires the workflow runs in the background with the event's data, and GAIA can notify you of the result. If the app has no trigger, run the workflow on a schedule instead.

faqs.question: What happens if a record matches both a real-time trigger and a scheduled run?
faqs.answer: Without a guard, it gets handled twice. Give each event an idempotency key or mark records as processed, and have the scheduled batch skip anything already handled. The same guard protects you from providers that deliver a webhook more than once.
